name: Adam Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm Elm Grove, 300 acres that were my father's. We grow chickens on contract for a big poultry processor, two sheds of 30,000 birds each, plus wheat and rapeseed, and we finish about 50 beef cattle over winter. First thing every morning I check the shed sensors on my phone, temperature, water, feed, then walk the sheds anyway because a phone can't smell a problem. I use AI all day: for the grain marketing, the shed data, the crop spraying plans, even to draft emails to the processor's field manager.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do things stand at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hannah cuts hair in the village three days a week, we've got Josiah who's twelve and Ellie who's eight, and a mortgage on the house. Last year I borrowed for a third shed, which is half built, so every spare penny is in concrete. We've got maybe ten days of money in the bank. I'm a church elder, and I'd say the Lord and the bank manager both get a lot of my prayers right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would surprise me. I see what it does every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm surprised, but I'd keep using it, because it still saves me hours. At the farmers' discussion group I'd say the useful bits are worth having even if the big promises weren't kept. I'm not one to post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the third shed has to pay for itself the old way. The loan is based on the processor renewing our contract next year, and that's a big if. If the processor cuts growers, we're stuck with a half-paid shed and no birds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the third shed as planned and push to get the contract renewed early. I'd keep using the AI for grain sales, because getting a better price for the wheat is real money. And we'd skip the family holiday this summer to keep cash in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous about the loan. Not about the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the processor doesn't renew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look for another processor, but there's only one within reach of our sheds. That's the risk with chickens. In poultry, you're a free man on paper and a tied man in practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Hannah feel about the shed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah backed it, but she'd tell you she prays harder than I do. She's the sensible one. She said if the shed fails she'll do five days at the salon, and I'd hate that.

say: I'd say I'm **surprised** but would keep using AI, since it saves hours.
I'd tell the discussion group the **useful bits** are still worth having.
think: I think the **third shed** must pay for itself the old way.
The loan rests on the processor **renewing the contract**, which isn't certain.
do: Finish the **third shed** and push for an early **contract renewal**.
Keep using AI for **grain sales** to get a better wheat price.
Skip the **family holiday** to keep cash in the account.
feel: **Nervous** about the loan, not about AI.
S0.quote: In poultry, you're a free man on paper and a tied man in practice.
fieldNote: Adam's stress is the **shed loan** and a single processor's contract.
He's a daily AI user who'd **keep using it** even in a plateau.
His wife's offer to **work more** is the household's backstop, and he dislikes it.
His **faith** is woven into how he talks about money worries.

steps.text: Finish the third poultry shed and seek an early contract renewal

Skip this summer's family holiday to keep cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That fits what I'm seeing. More tools, better tools, and the hands-on work stays mine for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for family farms to compete with the big boys, if we're willing to learn. I'd tell the discussion group that the farms who adapt will do fine. Nobody owes us a living; we have to earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it helps me. Better grain marketing, tighter feed control in the sheds, smarter spraying. If those save me even five percent on costs, the third shed loan gets easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move all the shed data and feed ordering onto one AI system in the first six months. I'd try an AI sprayer plan to cut chemical costs by a tenth. And I'd offer to help two neighbours set up the same tools, because a strong farming community helps everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with the loan sitting at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The processor gets the same tools, and they'd use them to set our contract prices tighter. They'd know my costs better than I do. That's the bit that could bite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody owes us a living. Does that apply to everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, yes. For someone like old Frank down the lane, who's seventy and never touched a computer, I'd want his family and the church to help him through. That's not a handout, that's neighbours.

say: I'd say it's a chance for **family farms** to compete, if they learn.
I'd tell people **nobody owes us** a living; we earn it.
think: I think it **helps me**: better grain prices, feed control and spraying.
Saving **five percent** on costs makes the shed loan easier.
do: Move shed data and **feed ordering** onto one AI system in six months.
Try an **AI sprayer plan** to cut chemical costs by a tenth.
Help **two neighbours** set up the same tools.
feel: **Optimistic**, with the **loan** at the back of his mind.
S1.quote: Nobody owes us a living; we have to earn it.
fieldNote: Adam sees Steady Disruption as **good for his margins**, which eases the loan.
He's alert to the **processor** using the same tools to squeeze growers.
His traditional view: **neighbours and church**, not government, help the old farmer.

steps.text: Put shed data and feed ordering on one AI system
Try an AI spraying plan to cut chemical costs by a tenth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028, then robots by 2031. That's fast, but I'd rather be ready than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test of whether family farms can move quickly. I'd say government should keep rules light so farmers can adapt, and help through apprenticeships, not handouts. I'd say it at church and the discussion group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the processor would use AGI to run everything and could drop small growers for big robotic ones by 2031. If I'm one of the most efficient growers, I'm safe; if not, I'm finished. With ten days of savings and a half-built shed, there's no room for mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate everything I can in the sheds and on the arable by 2029, borrowing a bit more if the bank would. I'd get the contract with the processor locked in for five years now. And I'd talk to Hannah about adding a fourth day at the salon to give us a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but I'd feel I've got some control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between AGI and robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get my sheds and records as sharp as anyone's. Thinking AI would do the processor's planning from 2028, so they'll know exactly who the best growers are. By 2031, when robots can catch and clean, I need to be on their list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Josiah and Ellie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Josiah and my daughter Ellie that the farm's going to look different, and we're going to make it work together. And I'd tell them God gave us brains to use them, so learning the new tools isn't wrong.

say: I'd say it's a test of whether **family farms** can move quickly.
I'd ask for **light rules** and apprenticeships, not handouts.
think: I think the processor may **drop small growers** by 2031.
With **ten days** of savings and a half-built shed, I can't afford mistakes.
do: **Automate** the sheds and arable by 2029, borrowing more if possible.
Lock in a **five-year contract** with the processor now.
Ask Hannah about a **fourth salon day** for a cushion.
S2.quote: God gave us brains to use them, so learning the new tools isn't wrong.
fieldNote: Adam expects the processor to **cut weaker growers**, and plans to be one of the best.
He'd **borrow more**, a risky move with thin savings.
His faith and **adaptability** sit together comfortably.
He'd ask his wife for **more hours**, which he disliked in the calm picture.

steps.text: Automate shed feeding and arable records by 2029
Lock in a five-year contract with the processor

Press for light farm rules and apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That gives me time to finish the shed and pay some of it down first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so farms should get ready now. I'd push the discussion group to plan for robots together. And I'd say government should stay out of the way and back apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. By 2031 the third shed is running and paid down a bit, and by 2034 I could have robots in it. The worry is the processor, as always, and the money between now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the shed, pay down the loan hard for two years, and then look at robot catchers and cleaners. I'd take an online course in poultry robotics over the winter. And I'd keep the arable going with AI planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. A bit of worry about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes first at Elm Grove between 2031 and 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side: grain marketing, ordering, the processor's planning. That's already half done by AI on my farm. Then the robots come for catching, cleaning and the feed rounds in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your stockmen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got one full-time man, Dave, who's been with us fifteen years. I'd want Dave trained on the robots, not replaced by them. Loyalty works both ways.

say: I'd say five years is **fair warning**, so farms should get ready now.
I'd push the discussion group to **plan for robots** together.
think: I think I'd **do well**, with the shed paid down by 2031.
The worry is **the processor** and money in between.

Look at **robot catchers** and cleaners after that.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a bit of worry about **money**.
S3.quote: I'd want Dave trained on the robots, not replaced by them.
fieldNote: With five years, Adam expects to **come out ahead**, which lowers his mood to uneasy.
He feels **loyalty** to his stockman Dave and wants him retrained.

steps.text: Pay down the third shed loan hard for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable for a man who's already using the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for any farmer willing to learn. I'd tell the young farmers to start now. And I'd say families and churches should help the ones who struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the best of the AGI pictures for me. The shed's paid off by then, the kids are grown, and I'd be ten years ahead of most farms on the tools. Money's tight now, but I'd have time to fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the farm the way I am. I'd save for robots over the decade instead of borrowing. And I'd help Josiah get an agricultural engineering apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. Looking forward to it, in a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship for Josiah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josiah loves the shed machines and takes apart anything with a motor. An apprenticeship teaches him the trade and pays him while he learns. That's better than debt from university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The processor, always. Ten years doesn't change that a big company holds the contract. I'd want a second processor within reach, but that's not something I can build myself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The shed loan would be fresh, the processor would be making big decisions fast, and there'd be no room for mistakes. What would help is a second poultry processor within reach, so we're not all tied to one company, and apprenticeships for young people who want to farm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of farmers lean on it, and it shapes how we see all this. I believe a man's work matters to God, whether it's done by hand or with a machine.

headlineQuote: I believe a man's work matters to God, whether it's done by hand or with a machine.
portrait: Adam farms **chickens on contract**, arable and beef on his father's 300 acres.
He uses **AI every day** and has ten days of savings after a shed loan.
He's a **church elder** who believes in self-reliance and helping neighbours.
He sees AI as a chance for **family farms**, but fears the single processor.
His mood is **anxious** in the plateau and fast AGI, and **uneasy** otherwise.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the **shed loan** would be fresh and the processor would move fast.
whatWouldHelp: A **second processor** within reach and **apprenticeships** for young farmers.
